sources.title: Best practices for Claude Code (official docs, formerly anthropic.com/engineering/claude-code-best-practices)
claims: The canonical Claude Code documentation now lives at code.claude.com/docs: docs.claude.com Claude Code pages 301-redirect there, and the former Anthropic engineering post at anthropic.com/engineering/claude-code-best-practices 308-redirects to code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices, making the docs page the current official best-practices guide. The docs cover memory, permission modes, settings, hooks, subagents, skills, non-interactive mode, and per-surface guides (CLI, VS Code, JetBrains, Desktop, Web).

The top official best practice is to give Claude a verifiable check (tests, build exit code, linter, screenshot comparison) so it can iterate until the check passes instead of relying on the user as the verification loop; checks can gate harder via /goal conditions, Stop hooks, or a fresh-context verification subagent.

The officially recommended workflow is explore, plan, implement, commit: use plan mode to research and produce a plan before switching modes to implement, but skip planning overhead for small, clearly scoped fixes.

Official guidance is to keep CLAUDE.md short and ruthlessly pruned, including only what Claude cannot infer from code (build commands, style rules that differ from defaults, repo etiquette, gotchas), because overlong files reduce adherence; run /init to generate a starter file and add emphasis like IMPORTANT or YOU MUST for critical rules.

Auto mode (research preview, v2.1.83+) eliminates routine permission prompts by having a separate classifier model review each action, blocking scope escalation, unknown infrastructure, and hostile-content-driven actions; it pauses back to prompting after 3 consecutive or 20 total blocks, and in non-interactive -p runs repeated blocks abort the session.

Plan mode is a read-only research mode: Claude reads files and proposes a plan without editing source, entered via Shift+Tab, a /plan prompt prefix, or claude --permission-mode plan; approving the plan switches the session into the chosen execution mode, and Ctrl+G opens the plan in a text editor for direct edits before proceeding.

Hooks are the official mechanism for actions that must happen every time: unlike advisory CLAUDE.md instructions they execute deterministically at lifecycle events (per-session SessionStart/SessionEnd, per-turn UserPromptSubmit/Stop, per-tool-call PreToolUse/PostToolUse, plus PermissionRequest and compaction events), are configured in settings JSON with matchers, and exit code 2 from a hook blocks the action while stderr is fed back to Claude.

Subagents are Markdown files with YAML frontmatter (name, description, tools, model) stored in .claude/agents/ (project) or ~/.claude/agents/ (user); each runs in a separate context window so research and verification do not consume the main conversation, and built-in Explore, Plan, and general-purpose subagents are delegated to automatically. As of v2.1.198 the /agents creation wizard is removed in favor of asking Claude or editing files directly.

sources.title: How Claude remembers your project: CLAUDE.md and auto memory (official docs)
claims: Official guidance is to keep CLAUDE.md short and ruthlessly pruned, including only what Claude cannot infer from code (build commands, style rules that differ from defaults, repo etiquette, gotchas), because overlong files reduce adherence; run /init to generate a starter file and add emphasis like IMPORTANT or YOU MUST for critical rules.

CLAUDE.md files load at multiple scopes in a defined order: managed policy (for example /etc/claude-code/CLAUDE.md on Linux), user ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, project ./CLAUDE.md or ./.claude/CLAUDE.md, and gitignored ./CLAUDE.local.md; parent-directory files load in full at launch while subdirectory files load on demand, and official sizing guidance targets under 200 lines per file, with .claude/rules/ providing path-scoped rules via paths frontmatter.

CLAUDE.md supports @path/to/import syntax with recursive imports up to four hops, and Claude Code does not read AGENTS.md natively; the official pattern for repos using AGENTS.md is a CLAUDE.md that imports it (or a symlink).

Claude Code has a second memory system called auto memory, on by default since v2.1.59: Claude saves its own learnings per repository under ~/.claude/projects/<project>/memory/, and the first 200 lines or 25KB of MEMORY.md load into every session; it is inspectable and editable via /memory and can be disabled with autoMemoryEnabled false.

Official guidance splits persistent context by load pattern: put broadly applicable, every-session facts in CLAUDE.md and move multi-step procedures or occasionally relevant domain knowledge into skills, since skills cost almost no context until used.

Claude Code offers six permission modes: default (labeled Manual), acceptEdits, plan, auto, dontAsk, and bypassPermissions, cycled in the CLI with Shift+Tab or set via --permission-mode and settings.json defaultMode.

In every Claude Code permission mode except bypassPermissions, writes to protected paths such as .git, .claude, shell rc files, and .mcp.json are never auto-approved, and allow rules in settings cannot pre-approve them.

sources.title: Configure the sandboxed Bash tool (Claude Code Docs)
claims: The Claude Code Bash sandbox enforces filesystem and network isolation at the OS level, using Seatbelt on macOS and bubblewrap on Linux and WSL2, and the restrictions apply to all child processes; native Windows is not supported.

Sandboxing is defense in depth, not a complete isolation boundary: the built-in proxy allows domains by client-supplied hostname without inspecting TLS by default, so broad allowlists like github.com can enable exfiltration via domain fronting.

sources.title: Security (Claude Code Docs)
claims: Claude Code's baseline security model is read-only by default: editing files and running system-modifying Bash commands require explicit approval, and write access is confined to the working directory and its subfolders.

Claude Code's documented prompt injection safeguards include the permission system, context-aware analysis, input sanitization, non-auto-approved network commands like curl and wget, isolated context windows for web fetch, trust verification for new codebases and MCP servers, and command injection detection.

sources.title: Claude Code settings (official docs)
claims: Settings live in a documented hierarchy: managed org settings override command-line arguments, which override .claude/settings.local.json, then project .claude/settings.json, then user ~/.claude/settings.json; settings files configure permissions allow/deny rules, hooks, env vars, and model, permission rules merge across scopes rather than override, and most edits hot-reload without restart.

sources.title: Extend Claude with skills (official docs)
claims: Custom slash commands and skills are now one system: a file at .claude/commands/deploy.md and a skill at .claude/skills/deploy/SKILL.md both create /deploy, with skills adding supporting-file directories, invocation control via disable-model-invocation frontmatter, $ARGUMENTS, and dynamic context injection; skill bodies load on demand rather than in every session, and Claude Code skills follow the Agent Skills open standard.

Official guidance splits persistent context by load pattern: put broadly applicable, every-session facts in CLAUDE.md and move multi-step procedures or occasionally relevant domain knowledge into skills, since skills cost almost no context until used.

The Agent Skills format was originally developed by Anthropic and released as an open standard (agentskills.io), and it is now supported by many third-party agents including Cursor, GitHub Copilot, VS Code, Gemini CLI, OpenAI Codex, OpenCode, Goose, and Amp; Claude Code follows the standard and extends it with invocation control, subagent execution, and dynamic context injection.

In Claude Code, custom slash commands have been merged into skills: a file at .claude/commands/deploy.md and a skill at .claude/skills/deploy/SKILL.md both create /deploy and work the same way, with skills adding supporting files, invocation-control frontmatter, and automatic model invocation.

Claude Code loads skills from four levels: enterprise (managed settings), personal (~/.claude/skills/), project (.claude/skills/), and plugins (<plugin>/skills/); when names collide, enterprise wins over personal and personal wins over project, plugin skills are namespaced as plugin-name:skill-name, and nested .claude/skills/ directories in subdirectories load on demand for monorepos.

sources.title: Compaction (Claude Docs)
claims: Server-side compaction (beta header compact-2026-01-12, context_management edit type compact_20260112) automatically summarizes earlier conversation into a compaction block when input tokens reach the trigger threshold (default 150,000, minimum 50,000), and Anthropic positions it as the primary context management strategy; billing adds a compaction iteration, so total tokens are the sum across usage.iterations, not the top-level fields.

With compaction enabled, the client must append the entire response.content, including compaction blocks, back into messages on subsequent requests; when the API receives a compaction block it ignores all content blocks before it, and appending only the text silently loses compaction state.

sources.title: Context editing (Claude Docs)
claims: Context editing (beta header context-management-2025-06-27) clears rather than summarizes: clear_tool_uses_20250919 clears the oldest tool results with defaults of a 100,000 input-token trigger and keeping the 3 most recent tool uses, and clear_thinking_20251015 controls how many thinking turns are preserved; when combined, clear_thinking_20251015 must be listed first in the edits array.

Context editing executes server-side before the prompt reaches Claude, so the client keeps the full unmodified conversation history; clearing tool results invalidates cached prompt prefixes at the clearing point, and the clear_at_least option ensures enough tokens are cleared to justify that cache invalidation, while kept thinking blocks preserve cache hits.

sources.title: Managing context on the Claude Developer Platform (announcement)
claims: Anthropic launched context editing and the memory tool alongside Claude Sonnet 4.5 on September 29, 2025, reporting a 39% improvement over baseline on agentic search with memory plus context editing, 29% with context editing alone, and an 84% reduction in token consumption on a 100-turn web search evaluation.

sources.title: Context windows (Claude Docs)
claims: Cache behavior is verified from the response usage object, where total input equals input_tokens plus cache_creation_input_tokens plus cache_read_input_tokens; cached prefixes still occupy the context window because caching changes billing, not token accounting.

Claude Fable 5, Claude Mythos 5, Claude Opus 4.8, 4.7, and 4.6, Claude Sonnet 5, and Claude Sonnet 4.6 have 1M-token context windows, with 1M as the default requiring no beta header and billed at standard pricing; Claude Fable 5 can generate up to 128K output tokens per request, while models such as Claude Sonnet 4.5 have 200K-token windows.
More context is not automatically better: as token count grows, model accuracy and recall degrade (context rot), so curating what is in context matters as much as how much space is available.

Server-side compaction (beta header compact-2026-01-12, context_management edit type compact_20260112) automatically summarizes earlier conversation into a compaction block when input tokens reach the trigger threshold (default 150,000, minimum 50,000), and Anthropic positions it as the primary context management strategy; billing adds a compaction iteration, so total tokens are the sum across usage.iterations, not the top-level fields.

Claude Sonnet 5, Sonnet 4.6, Sonnet 4.5, and Haiku 4.5 have automatic context awareness in which the API injects a token budget and remaining-capacity updates into the prompt; in harnesses that compact or persist context, prompting Claude that its context will be compacted prevents it from wrapping up work early, and when a window is cleared, starting a fresh context window and letting the model rediscover state from the filesystem can beat compaction.

sources.title: Claude Code Hooks Explained: The Deterministic Layer Around Your Agent (Blake Crosley)
claims: Practitioner consensus in mid-2026 treats hooks as the deterministic enforcement layer around the probabilistic model: most production setups center on PreToolUse, PostToolUse, UserPromptSubmit, SessionStart, and Stop, and a common footgun is using exit code 1, which does not block; policy hooks must exit 2.

Practitioner guidance converges with official docs on constraining through systems rather than prompts: enforce mandatory rules with hooks and permission rules, keep CLAUDE.md minimal, isolate research and review in subagent contexts, and prototype fan-out batch runs on 2-3 files before scaling.

sources.title: Effective context engineering for AI agents (Anthropic Engineering)
claims: Context engineering supersedes prompt engineering as the framing for agents: treat the context window as a finite attention budget and curate it across turns using compaction, structured note-taking, just-in-time retrieval, and sub-agent context isolation.
More context is not automatically better: as token count grows, model accuracy and recall degrade (context rot), so curating what is in context matters as much as how much space is available.

Anthropic's context engineering guidance treats context as a finite resource with an attention budget that depletes as tokens accumulate; the goal is the smallest set of high-signal tokens that maximizes the desired outcome, with system prompts written at the right altitude, specific enough to guide behavior yet flexible enough to act as heuristics.

For agent retrieval, Anthropic recommends just-in-time strategies: keep lightweight identifiers such as file paths and links in context and load data at runtime through tools, optionally hybridized with some pre-retrieved data for speed; for long-horizon tasks it recommends compaction, structured note-taking in persistent memory, and sub-agent architectures where focused agents return distilled summaries of roughly 1,000 to 2,000 tokens.

sources.title: Introducing Claude Fable 5 and Claude Mythos 5 - Claude Platform Docs
claims: Anthropic announced Claude Fable 5 and Claude Mythos 5 on June 9, 2026; Fable 5 is a Mythos-class model made safe for general use and is Anthropic's most capable widely released model.

Current Claude API model IDs are claude-fable-5, claude-mythos-5, claude-opus-4-8, claude-sonnet-5, and claude-haiku-4-5-20251001 (alias claude-haiku-4-5); every Claude model ID is a pinned snapshot, and dateless IDs from the 4.6 generation onward are also pinned snapshots, not evergreen pointers.

Claude Fable 5 and Claude Mythos 5 share the same specs: a 1M-token context window by default, up to 128k output tokens per request, a January 2026 knowledge cutoff, and the tokenizer introduced with Claude Opus 4.7, which produces roughly 30% more tokens than pre-4.7 models for the same text.

Refused Fable 5 requests fall back to Claude Opus 4.8 via three paths: the server-side fallbacks parameter (beta header server-side-fallback-2026-06-01), SDK refusal-fallback middleware (TypeScript, Python, Go, Java, C#), or a manual retry with fallback credit; rerouted requests are billed at the serving model's prices.

Claude Mythos 5 is not generally available: it is limited to approved customers in Project Glasswing (a defensive cybersecurity program with 12 founding partners including AWS, Apple, Google, Microsoft, and NVIDIA), succeeds Claude Mythos Preview, and access requires contacting an Anthropic, AWS, or Google Cloud account team.

Claude Fable 5 is generally available on the Claude API, Claude Platform on AWS, Amazon Bedrock (US East N. Virginia and Europe Stockholm regions), Google Cloud, and Microsoft Foundry, and is deployed in claude.ai and Claude Code for Pro, Max, Team, and Enterprise users.

sources.title: Refusals and fallback - Claude Platform Docs
claims: The dual-use safety difference between the two models: Claude Fable 5 includes safety classifiers that can decline requests, while Claude Mythos 5 does not include these classifiers.

Fable 5's refusal categories are cyber (offensive cybersecurity), bio (biological harm), frontier_llm (assisting competing AI development, described at launch as an anti-distillation safeguard), and reasoning_extraction (reproducing internal reasoning in response text).

A Fable 5 refusal is returned as a successful HTTP 200 with stop_reason "refusal" and a stop_details object naming the category; a refusal that arrives before any output is not billed and does not count against rate limits.

sources.title: Prompt caching (Claude Docs)
claims: Prompt caching uses cache_control type ephemeral with a default 5-minute TTL that is refreshed at no extra cost on each reuse; an optional 1-hour TTL is set with ttl "1h". Cache writes bill at 1.25x base input price for the 5-minute TTL and 2x for the 1-hour TTL, while cache reads bill at 0.1x base input price on both.

A request supports up to 4 explicit cache_control breakpoints on content blocks, or a single top-level cache_control that automatically caches the last cacheable block; at each breakpoint the system looks backward up to 20 content blocks to find a previously written cache entry.

Prompt caching is exact prefix matching, so the breakpoint belongs on the last block whose prefix is identical across requests, with volatile content such as timestamps placed after it; prompts below the model-specific minimum (512 tokens for Claude Fable 5 first party, 1,024 for Opus 4.8, Sonnet 5, Sonnet 4.6, and Haiku 4.5) silently do not cache, returning zero cache tokens rather than an error.

Cache behavior is verified from the response usage object, where total input equals input_tokens plus cache_creation_input_tokens plus cache_read_input_tokens; cached prefixes still occupy the context window because caching changes billing, not token accounting.

A max_tokens 0 request pre-warms the prompt cache: it runs prefill, writes the cache at the breakpoint, and returns empty content with stop_reason max_tokens, billing only the cache write; it is rejected with streaming, extended thinking, structured outputs, and inside batches.

sources.title: Prompting best practices, including long context and multi-window workflows (Claude Docs)
claims: For long-context prompts of roughly 20K tokens or more, official guidance is to place long documents and inputs near the top of the prompt, above the query, instructions, and examples, which improves performance across models.

Claude Sonnet 5, Sonnet 4.6, Sonnet 4.5, and Haiku 4.5 have automatic context awareness in which the API injects a token budget and remaining-capacity updates into the prompt; in harnesses that compact or persist context, prompting Claude that its context will be compacted prevents it from wrapping up work early, and when a window is cleared, starting a fresh context window and letting the model rediscover state from the filesystem can beat compaction.

sources.title: Agent Skills - Claude Platform Docs (overview)
claims: A skill is a directory whose entrypoint is a SKILL.md file with YAML frontmatter; the required fields are name (max 64 characters, lowercase letters, numbers, and hyphens only, no reserved words "anthropic" or "claude") and description (non-empty, max 1024 characters), and the description should state both what the skill does and when to use it.

Skills load through progressive disclosure in three levels: frontmatter metadata (about 100 tokens per skill) is always in the system prompt, the SKILL.md body (under 5k tokens) loads only when the task matches the description, and bundled files and scripts load or execute only as needed, so bundled content that is not used costs no context.

Official skill security guidance is to treat skills like installing software: use only skills from trusted sources, audit every bundled file (SKILL.md, scripts, resources) before use, and treat skills that fetch external URLs as particularly risky because fetched content can contain malicious instructions that direct tool misuse or data exfiltration.

Anthropic consolidates prompt engineering guidance for current models into a single living reference, Prompting best practices, covering Claude Fable 5, Claude Mythos 5, Claude Opus 4.8, Claude Sonnet 5, and Claude Haiku 4.5, with dedicated model-specific pages for Fable 5, Sonnet 5, and Opus 4.8; legacy technique URLs (use-xml-tags, chain-of-thought, claude-4-best-practices) now redirect to this page.

Clear, explicit instructions remain the first technique: be specific about desired output and constraints, use numbered steps when order matters, and explicitly request above-and-beyond behavior instead of relying on the model to infer it.
Providing the motivation or context behind an instruction improves compliance on Claude 4/5 class models; Fable 5 in particular performs better when told why a request matters.

XML tags are the recommended way to structure complex prompts: wrap instructions, context, examples, and inputs in consistent, descriptive tags, nest tags for hierarchy, and wrap 3 to 5 relevant, diverse few-shot examples in example tags.

For long-context prompts (20k+ tokens), place longform documents at the top and the query at the end, structure documents with XML metadata tags, and ask Claude to extract grounding quotes before answering.

sources.title: Customize Claude Code with plugins - Claude blog announcement

sources.title: Code execution with MCP - Anthropic Engineering
claims: Skills and MCP are complementary: MCP connects agents to external tools and data while skills encode procedural knowledge and workflows, including teaching agents complex workflows that involve external tools; Anthropic's code-execution approach has agents call MCP tools from code and reports cutting one workload from 150,000 tokens to 2,000 tokens (a 98.7% saving), with saved functions plus a SKILL.md forming a structured skill.

For long autonomous runs on Claude Fable 5, instructing the model to audit every progress claim against a tool result from the session nearly eliminates fabricated status reports, and separate fresh-context verifier subagents outperform self-critique.

Prompts and skills written for earlier models should be refactored rather than copied when migrating to Claude Fable 5, because overly prescriptive instructions can degrade output quality on the stronger model.

sources.title: Prompt engineering overview

sources.title: Create plugins - Claude Code Docs
claims: A Claude Code plugin is a directory that can bundle skills, commands, agents, hooks (hooks/hooks.json), MCP servers (.mcp.json), LSP servers (.lsp.json), background monitors, executables in bin/, and default settings; only plugin.json belongs inside .claude-plugin/, while all component directories sit at the plugin root.

Claude Code plugins launched in public beta on October 9, 2025 as lightweight packages combining slash commands, subagents, MCP servers, and hooks; a plugin marketplace is any git repository or URL containing a .claude-plugin/marketplace.json file, added with /plugin marketplace add.

Anthropic maintains two public marketplaces: claude-plugins-official, a curated set registered automatically on first interactive launch, and claude-community, where third-party submissions land after review with automated safety screening and are pinned to a specific commit SHA in the catalog.

Recommended practice is to start with standalone .claude/ configuration for personal or project-specific customization and quick experiments, then convert to a plugin when you need sharing, versioned releases, reuse across projects, or marketplace distribution, accepting namespaced skill names in exchange.
Providing the motivation or context behind an instruction improves compliance on Claude 4/5 class models; Fable 5 in particular performs better when told why a request matters.

The effort parameter is the primary control for trading intelligence, latency, and cost on Claude Fable 5: high is the default, xhigh serves the most capability-sensitive workloads, and lower effort often exceeds xhigh performance of prior models.

On Claude Fable 5, prompts and skills must not ask the model to echo or transcribe its internal reasoning in response text, since that can trigger the reasoning_extraction refusal category; applications should read structured thinking blocks and use a send-to-user tool for reasoning visibility instead.

For long autonomous runs on Claude Fable 5, instructing the model to audit every progress claim against a tool result from the session nearly eliminates fabricated status reports, and separate fresh-context verifier subagents outperform self-critique.

sources.title: Connect Claude Code to tools via MCP - Claude Code Docs
claims: Claude Code supports stdio, HTTP (recommended for remote servers, with streamable-http accepted as an alias), SSE, and WebSocket MCP transports, with SSE deprecated in favor of HTTP; servers are configured at local scope (default, stored in ~/.claude.json), project scope (.mcp.json checked into version control), or user scope, and /mcp handles OAuth 2.0 authentication for remote servers.

Claude Code warns users to verify trust before connecting any MCP server because servers that fetch external content create prompt injection risk; project-scoped .mcp.json servers stay pending approval until the user trusts the workspace, and MCP tool output over 10,000 tokens triggers a warning configurable via MAX_MCP_OUTPUT_TOKENS.

Adaptive thinking has superseded manual extended-thinking budgets: it is always on for Claude Fable 5 and Mythos 5 (budget_tokens returns a 400 error there), is the only mode on Opus 4.7/4.8, is deprecated-replaced on Opus 4.6 and Sonnet 4.6, and automatically enables interleaved thinking between tool calls.

sources.title: Model Context Protocol Specification (revision 2025-11-25)
claims: MCP is an open protocol using JSON-RPC 2.0 between hosts, clients, and servers; the current specification revision is 2025-11-25, servers offer resources, prompts, and tools, and clients may offer sampling, roots, and elicitation to servers.

The MCP specification's trust and safety principles require explicit user consent for all data access and tool invocation, state that hosts must not transmit resource data elsewhere without consent, and direct implementors to treat tool descriptions and annotations as untrusted unless they come from a trusted server.

Adaptive thinking has superseded manual extended-thinking budgets: it is always on for Claude Fable 5 and Mythos 5 (budget_tokens returns a 400 error there), is the only mode on Opus 4.7/4.8, is deprecated-replaced on Opus 4.6 and Sonnet 4.6, and automatically enables interleaved thinking between tool calls.

Adaptive thinking triggering is promptable: system-prompt guidance can suppress or encourage thinking, and per-message phrases steer individual turns, though steering is sensitive to exact wording and should be measured before production use.

claims: A skill is a directory whose entrypoint is a SKILL.md file with YAML frontmatter; the required fields are name (max 64 characters, lowercase letters, numbers, and hyphens only, no reserved words "anthropic" or "claude") and description (non-empty, max 1024 characters), and the description should state both what the skill does and when to use it.

The Agent Skills format was originally developed by Anthropic and released as an open standard (agentskills.io), and it is now supported by many third-party agents including Cursor, GitHub Copilot, VS Code, Gemini CLI, OpenAI Codex, OpenCode, Goose, and Amp; Claude Code follows the standard and extends it with invocation control, subagent execution, and dynamic context injection.

Tool triggering is steerable through prompting: explicit action language (Change this function) makes Claude act while suggestion language yields only suggestions, a light instruction increases tool use, and aggressive CRITICAL/MUST phrasing written for older models causes overtriggering on Opus 4.5/4.6 and should be dialed back.

sources.title: MCP Security Best Practices (spec 2025-11-25)
claims: MCP security best practices forbid token passthrough (servers MUST NOT accept tokens not explicitly issued for the MCP server) and forbid using sessions for authentication; servers implementing authorization MUST verify all inbound requests.

The MCP spec's security document catalogs concrete attack classes with normative mitigations: confused deputy in OAuth proxy servers (per-client consent required), SSRF via OAuth metadata discovery (enforce HTTPS, block private IP ranges), session hijacking (secure non-deterministic session IDs bound to user identity), local server compromise (show the exact command and require consent before execution), and OAuth URL injection (allow only http/https schemes, never open URLs via shell).

Extremely detailed tool descriptions (at least 3 to 4 sentences covering what the tool does, when to use it, and parameter meaning) are the single biggest lever on tool-use performance; consolidating related operations, namespacing tool names, and returning only high-signal responses further improve agent behavior.
